narrative:
The model estimates a 67% chance that you will leave, so the promotion was denied because the organization sees you as a high flight risk. This is not a judgment of your ability; it means the predicted cost of promoting someone likely to exit outweighed the expected benefit.

The strongest signal was that you have received other job opportunities. That pushed the prediction toward leaving more than any other factor. Among employees predicted to stay, only about one in four had outside opportunities, so your situation stands out as a retention warning.

Your overall experience—1–5 years—was the second most important factor, but it pushed in the opposite direction, toward staying. That range is common among employees expected to stay, so it softened the risk somewhat.

The third factor was your sector. Working in the “other” sector added a moderate push toward leaving, because employees predicted to stay are more often in medical or education than in other sectors.

Before finalizing denial, your manager should discuss your intentions, the outside opportunities you have, and whether a promotion would change your plans. You should clarify your commitment and career expectations. The organization should consider a retention plan, clearer growth path, and support; you should weigh whether to stay or pursue those other offers.
